name: United States
headline: Americans have an enforced legal right to copies of their records, but providers and insurers decide most sharing, and health apps sit outside HIPAA.

access.summary: HIPAA gives a right to the whole designated record set within 30 days at a cost-based fee, and OCR has brought 55 right of access enforcement actions. There is no national record: 65% used a portal in 2024, and 59% had more than one.
detail: Under 45 CFR 164.524 a provider or health plan must act on an access request within 30 days, with one 30-day extension. If the record is held electronically and readily producible, the patient gets it in the electronic form and format they ask for. Fees may cover only labor, supplies and postage.
OCR enforces the right. Its 55th Right of Access action, announced on August 27, 2026, fined Azul Vision $50,000 after a patient waited almost two years for records requested in January 2023.

Access runs provider by provider. In 2024, 65% of people were offered and used an online record or portal and 57% used an app. But 59% had several portals, and only 7% used an app to combine them (ASTP Data Brief 77).
OCR's regulatory agenda lists a proposed rule, planned for November 2026, on how long covered entities have to answer access requests, according to an HCCA report.

control.summary: HIPAA lets providers and plans share records for treatment, payment and operations without consent, and they may refuse restriction requests. A block on items paid in full and a six-year disclosure log that omits routine sharing put the cell at the top of its band.
detail: 45 CFR 164.506 says a covered entity may use or disclose health information for treatment, payment and health care operations. Asking for consent is optional for the provider. It is not a patient right.
Under 164.522 a patient may ask for restrictions, but the covered entity is not required to agree. The one exception: an item the patient paid for in full can be kept from their health plan.
The accounting of disclosures under 164.528 covers six years but excludes disclosures for treatment, payment and operations. So the patient cannot see most routine sharing.

Substance use disorder records are the exception. The 2024 Part 2 rule, with compliance from February 16, 2026, lets a patient give one written consent for future treatment, payment and operations uses. Payers must let patients opt out of the Provider Access API from January 2027, a requirement not yet in force.

privacy.summary: HIPAA is enforced, with breach reporting and fines, but breaches are vast: 397 large breaches exposed 33.77 million people in the first half of 2026. The Security Rule overhaul proposed in January 2025 now has a July 2027 target.
detail: HIPAA covers providers, health plans, clearinghouses and their business associates. Breaches affecting 500 or more people are reported to HHS. From January to June 2026 there were 397 such breaches affecting 33.77 million people, 343 of them hacking or IT incidents (HIPAA Journal tally of HHS OCR breach reports).

The largest health breach on record, at Change Healthcare in 2024, affected about 192.7 million people. OCR announced seven settlements in the first half of 2026, each with a fine for a missing risk analysis.
The Security Rule update proposed on January 6, 2025 is not final. The Unified Agenda lists it as a long-term action with final action in July 2027.

Police can get records by court order, subpoena or administrative request under 164.512(f). A federal court vacated most of the 2024 reproductive health privacy rule on June 18, 2025 (Purl v. HHS). Texas requires electronic health records to be stored in the US from January 1, 2026.

commercial.summary: Inside HIPAA, marketing and any sale of patient data need written authorization. But de-identified data falls outside the law, and health apps answer mainly to an FTC breach-notice rule and a few state laws such as Washington's.
detail: Under 164.508 a covered entity needs authorization for marketing, except face-to-face talks and nominal gifts, and for any sale of health information. The form must say the entity is being paid.
Data that meets the de-identification standard in 164.514 is no longer individually identifiable health information. It can be used or sold without the patient's permission.
Apps and devices outside HIPAA fall under the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, updated in April 2024 to cover health apps. It requires notice of breaches. It does not ban sharing.

States fill gaps unevenly. Washington's My Health My Data Act has made it unlawful since March 31, 2024 to sell consumer health data without a signed authorization. New York's governor vetoed a similar bill on December 19, 2025.

journey.summary: Exchange is growing: 76% of hospitals did all four exchange tasks in 2025, and TEFCA went from 10 million to over 1 billion records in under a year. There is still no national record, and payer APIs are due in 2027.
detail: There is no national EHR. Records move through vendor networks, regional exchanges and TEFCA, the federal framework. HHS said on June 26, 2026 that TEFCA exchange grew from 10 million to more than 1 billion records in under a year, and it hired a contractor to check network rules.
In 2025, 96% of hospitals sent, 93% received and 94% queried for outside records, but only 79% integrated them. 76% did all four, up from 70% in 2023 (ASTP).

Public health links are strong. In 2024, 97% of hospitals reported immunizations electronically and 94% sent lab results. Virtually all pharmacies accept e-prescriptions, and 92% of prescribers send them.
Insurers lag. CMS-0057-F requires Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP and marketplace plans to run Patient Access, Provider Access and payer-to-payer FHIR APIs, with most deadlines on January 1, 2027.

clinical.summary: HIPAA allows sharing for treatment without consent, so the limits are technical. In 2023, 71% of hospitals had routine access to outside records at the point of care, but only 42% said clinicians routinely used them.
detail: ASTP's 2023 hospital survey found 71% of hospitals routinely had the clinical information they needed from outside providers when treating patients. Only 42% said clinicians routinely used it. Just 16% sent care summaries to most long-term care providers.
Medication history is better connected: 92% of prescribers e-prescribe and virtually all pharmacies accept e-prescriptions.

HHS announced a crackdown on information blocking on September 3, 2025. In early 2026 ASTP said it was issuing notices of investigation to health IT developers, who face fines of up to $1 million per violation. Nearly 1,600 complaints had been filed by February 2026 (Holland & Knight).
Small and independent hospitals exchange less, so what a clinician sees depends on where the patient is treated.

research.summary: An IRB or privacy board can waive the patient's authorization when risk is minimal, and de-identified data needs no consent, so there is no general opt-out. Three safeguards lift the cell: board review, Certificates of Confidentiality and a broad-consent route.
detail: Under 164.512(i) health information can be used for research without authorization if an IRB or privacy board finds no more than minimal privacy risk and that the research could not practicably be done without the waiver.
De-identified data under 164.514 is outside HIPAA, so large datasets are built without asking patients. None of the federal rules reviewed gives a general opt-out.

The Common Rule (45 CFR 46.116) requires informed consent for federally funded research, allows broad consent for storing and reusing identifiable data and specimens, and lets an IRB waive consent on similar criteria.
Since 2017, NIH-funded research meeting set criteria is automatically covered by a Certificate of Confidentiality, which bars disclosure of identifiable research data without consent.

ai.summary: FDA regulates AI devices, listing about 1,600, and has final guidance on change control plans. But HHS proposed removing the only federal AI transparency rule for certified EHRs, and January 2026 guidance took more decision support software out of oversight.
detail: FDA's public list of AI-enabled devices (page current as of September 4, 2026) has about 1,600 entries, with decisions through June 2026. FDA says it will explore tagging devices that use large language models.
FDA's final guidance on predetermined change control plans for AI device software (page dated August 2025) lets makers get planned model updates authorized in advance.

HTI-5, proposed on December 29, 2025, would remove 34 of 60 EHR certification criteria and strip the AI model card requirements from decision support. Comments closed on February 27, 2026, and no final rule was found. In January 2026 FDA also issued guidance narrowing oversight of decision support and wellness software.

States add rules. California AB 3030 requires a disclaimer on AI-written patient messages unless a clinician reviewed them. Texas SB 1188 requires practitioners to review AI-made records and tell patients when they use AI for diagnosis.
